I have a quick question about repairConfiguration: after reading section 5.7 and 11.1 and irace --help, I am not entirely sure how to include such a repair function when using the config files (not the R interface). Is this currently possible? If so, where would I have to make edit? I could not find many traces of repairConfiguration in the tmpl files.

What I am trying to do: 10 real numbers \in (0,1) are sorted from smallest to largest element. This is a minor optimisation on the user side, as I do not want to burden irace with sampling permutations.

An alternative should be to hardcode this as a constraint, however, this might sometimes result in a lot of resampling on irace's side before a valid configuration is found.

Thank you!

Best wishes,
Markus

messages.subject: Re: [irace-package] Re: irace version 2.2
messages.body_plain:
Hi Markus,

Currently, repairConfiguration needs to be an R function. You can still specify
it in the scenario.txt file. That is, you can directly write the code from
Section 5.7 into your scenario.txt file. I'll update the user guide to make
this clear. Thanks!

We could make it work like target-runner (which can be a function or an
executable), but we will need to define an exchange format since input/output
is more complex. I'm also afraid that calling a script for each configuration
may be too slow (but you can still use system2 to call a script from
repairConfiguration).

Please, let me know whether it works for you and any other comments or suggestions.

Cheers,

Manuel.

messages.subject: Re: [irace-package] testNbElites
messages.body_plain:
Hi Markus,

On 15/05/17 10:18, M. Wagner wrote:
> I wonder about the semantics of "testing" right now.
>
> In my setup, I use
>
> testNbElites = 10
> testIterationElites = 1
>
> and the irace run with 1000 experiments end up having a few iterations. In the
> end, testing is done on 5 configurations (not on a number that is closer to
> 5*10). Each of the iterations returns the same "Best configuration", so the
> following question: which instances are tested in my case? :) Below is an example.

The way this works is explained in Sect 7. If you can point out what part is
not clear, perhaps I can re-write it in a clearer way.

In a nutshell, testIterationElites controls whether only the final elites or
also the elites at each iteration are tested. The elites are those
configurations that are still alive at the end of a race, which can be even
just one. testNbElites is a maximum in the number of elites tested from each
iteration, the actual number of elites at any particular iteration may be
smaller. Finally, we only test each configuration once. That is, if an elite
appears in iteration 2 and survives until the end, it is only tested once. By
"testing", we mean that a configuration is evaluated on all test instances as
provided by testInstancesDir/testInstancesFile.

> ps: iteration count bug? see below: "Iteration 4 of 5", "Iteration 6 of 6", ...

There is an "Iteration 5 of 5" between those two. Iterated F-race estimates a
minimum number of iterations to perform, however, depending on what happens
while running, there may enough budget left to keep running, thus irace adjusts
itself to keep going on. The iteration number also controls how exploratory the
sampling is, thus sometimes irace may skip iterations because one particular
iteration is not feasible with the remaining budget. This is all explained and
specified in the ORP paper.

Cheers,

Manuel.

On 16/05/17 08:46, M. Wagner wrote:
>     We could make it work like target-runner (which can be a function or an
>     executable), but we will need to define an exchange format since input/output
>     is more complex. I'm also afraid that calling a script for each configuration
>     may be too slow (but you can still use system2 to call a script from
>     repairConfiguration).
>
>
> This might indeed be a significant overhead if the experiment itself is very short.
>
> In case you will have a template for this in the future, maybe a comment on
> this might suffice? "Note that pre-processing of configurations can cost time."
> (or so... processing cannot come for free, although processing in R might be
> the fastest if irace is in R)

In fact, for 2.4 we will byte-compile the R code provided by the user to speed
it up a little bit, so the difference between using R and using an external
script will grow larger.

But I don't understand what you mean by a template. What do you want to see in
such template?

> Well, it depends a bit on irace's logic: given the original config C1 and the
> modified C2, do you just overwrite C1 with C2 internally (pretending C1 never
> existed) and then feed it to target-runner? Well, if there is some
> self-adaptation or model-based search (yes: I have no idea what is inside
> irace), then this overwriting might go against the internal logic a bit.

After C1 is generated, the repairConfiguration function is called and C1 is
overwritten. Nothing else in irace sees the original C1, it is never evaluated.
It is as if irace actually generated the repaired C1. This is a pure repair of
representation constraints.

>     Please, let me know whether it works for you and any other comments or
>     suggestions.
>
>
> For me as a non-R user, I will wait for the updated user guide :) This is not
> urgent: I resorted to sorting the parameters in my external program. This might
> not be optimal but it works okay.

What do you expect to be updated in the user guide? I'm not sure what you refer to.

Sorting the parameters in your external program is very sub-optimal, because
irace believes that the original configuration is OK and it will try to
generate similar ones. This may be ok or terribly deceptive depending on the
problem.

Sorting the parameters may be one or two lines in R. (Admittedly, I'm not sure
what you mean by "sorting" the parameters). You can also write your R code in
C++ (http://www.rcpp.org/).

Alternatively, I can try to provide a general-purpose R function that takes a
configuration, calls a script like target-runner is called, then parses the
output of the script, which should return a repaired command-line, and converts
this to the internal representation used by irace. You'll just need to write
the script (in whatever language you wish) that does the repairing. As I say
above, this will be slower than having a pure R repair function, but it may be
fast enough for your purposes.

I'm happy to implement this if it will be useful to you.

Cheers,

Manuel.

Currently, repairConfiguration cannot be a script, so it cannot be like
target-runner.tmpl.  repairConfiguration needs to be defined in the
scenario.txt file, see below.

>> What do you expect to be updated in the user guide? I'm not sure what you refer to.
>
> This was referring to this earlier comment of yours: “That is, you can directly write the code from Section 5.7 into your scenario.txt file. I'll update the user guide to make this clear. Thanks!"

OK, this will be done for the next version.

> Sorting: given the 9 values, I just sort them based on the value, i.e., from smallest to largest.
> Small example: p1=0.4 p2=0.5 p3=0.1 ==> 0.1 0.4 0.5

If this is all you need to do, this repair function should do the trick:

repairConfiguration = function (configuration, parameters, digits)
{
   columns <- c("p1","p2","p3")
   # cat("Before"); print(configuration)
   configuration[columns] <- sort(configuration[columns])
   # cat("After"); print(configuration)
   return(configuration)
}

You can uncomment the two print() lines to check that it works as you expect.
Just copy the above code into your scenario.txt file.

> Current point where I am stuck: how exactly could I insert the R code, and where? You said “You can still specify it in the scenario.txt file.”, however, my scenario.txt seems to be missing any reference to repair functions. Is this maybe because I update from an earlier irace version to 2.3 and the template files were not overwritten?

Ops, I forgot to update the scenario.txt template by adding
repairConfiguration. Good catch! It'll be fixed in the next version. I see now
that this may be causing a lot of the confusion about templates. I added to
scenario.txt.tmpl the following lines:

## User-defined R function that takes a configuration generated by irace and
## repairs it.
# repairConfiguration = ""

You can copy the code from the user-guide or from above into scenario.txt or
you can uncomment the last line above and replace "" with function(...) {}
(Little secret: the scenario.txt is actually R code. You can even load
packages, and do all kinds of crazy stuff there.)

>> Alternatively, I can try to provide a general-purpose R function that takes a configuration, calls a script like target-runner is called, then parses the output of the script, which should return a repaired command-line, and converts this to the internal representation used by irace. You'll just need to write the script (in whatever language you wish) that does the repairing. As I say above, this will be slower than having a pure R repair function, but it may be fast enough for your purposes.
>
> Sounds excellent!

Actually, if you try the function above (use --check for a quick check), it may
already do what you need.

Cheers,

Manuel.

messages.subject: Re: [irace-package] testNbElites
messages.body_plain:
On 16/05/17 13:35, M. Wagner wrote:
> Since you state “can be further sorted according to their mean value” —>
> this is happening now, right? I am just a little curious when the word “can”
> is used.

This happens already when we print out the elites at the end of each
iteration/race and at the end before testing (Best configurations).

> Since you state “mean value or sum of ranks” —> which one is it, or how
> would I know which criteria is used? Just curious…

This depends on the testType (--test-type). If you use the F-test (the
default), they are sorted according to their sum of ranks (which is the same as
mean rank in this context) If you use the t-test, they are sorted according to
the mean value.

> The reason I keep asking: I had another irace run where the “tested
> configurations” ended up being sorted (almost perfectly) the wrong way
> around. Yes, I know there is a big random component in my setup. My testing
> used 1 million repetitions (!) then (in the testing only!) and the “further
> down ones” in the list of “tested configurations” ended up being better than
> the “further up ones” (note that I am avoiding the words “top”/“worst”
> here). Yes, due to randomness… still, it was worth asking whether there is
> an underlying system behind the way the configurations are listed (yes,
> based on the experiments, the races, the randomness, and then sorting). Ok.

The system is as follows (and I'm going to update the output of irace to make
this obvious, thanks for pointing it out):

* Elite configurations and the final "# Best configurations" are sorted from
best to worst (on the subset of the training set that they have been evaluated
on) according to sum of ranks (F-test) or mean value (t-test).

* Other printouts of configurations are either in the order in which they were
generated or with an arbitrary order.

Thus, the configurations to be tested (the list after "# Testing
configurations:") may be in an arbitrary order. Actually, I'm not sure we can
print any sensible order when mixing iteration-elites from different
iterations, since an elite that was discarded in iteration 3 will have results
on different training instances than an elite that was discarded in iteration
6. Note that we print these configurations to be tested before evaluating them
on the test instances. We don't try to sort them after testing and the final "#
Testing results" matrix is not sorted according to performance. Perhaps it
would be useful to sort it? On the other hand, one should not do any further
tuning or selection based on the test results; otherwise you are doing tuning
on the test instances, which betrays the reason for separating training and
testing instances. It will be methodologically wrong to select the best
configuration among the elites according to the results on the test instances.

Ideally, if you compare the testing results of the elites that survived until
the end to testing results of the elites that were discarded before reaching
the end, the former should have a higher performance. There are many reasons
this may not be true (the latter were not evaluated on as many instances as the
former and the additional instances are quite different from the common ones,
the train instances may actually not be correlated with the test instances,
randomness/unlucky runs may have killed early the best configurations), but it
tends to be rare that this happens outside artificial setups.

If you send me the irace.Rdata file privately, it will be easy to check what
went wrong.

Perhaps we can print a final report on average performance on training vs
testing for all elites tested at the end.

Cheers,

Manuel.

messages.body_plain:
On 18/05/17 01:57, M. Wagner wrote:
> A very good point! I was very tempted to support the sorting, however, I agree
> with you. Better don’t sort it. Some people might have very good reasons to
> pick the best from the training set (I have some right now ;), but it is better
> to leave them either in the current semi-unsorted order.

Just to be completely clear. It is OK to pick the best from the *training* set
results. Those are the configurations printed after the line:

# Best configurations (first number is the configuration ID; sorted from best
to worst according to the sum of ranks)

and they are sorted from best (on the training set) to worst (note the new text
explaining the sorting).

What is not OK is to pick the best by looking at the *test* set results. They
are there just to let you know what happens for "unseen" instances not tuned for.

It is like doing 30 runs to calculate mean performance, but then re-running
those runs that are pretty bad. Yes, one would get better results but also fool
one-self about what is the actual mean performance.

Actually, the ideal way would be to do what ML people do: have three sets,
training, validation and test, then do cross-validation with various tuning
runs and pick the best configuration according to the validation set, then
compare with other algorithms on the test set (but not do more selection or
tuning). However, this will be extremely expensive in most real-world scenarios
and probably hard to explain to typical reviewers. First let's get to the point
where almost everybody accepts the training/test separation and automatic
configuration as a default step in algorithm design and analysis :)

Cheers,

Manuel.

messages.subject: irace 2.3 with multiple objectives (target-evaluator)
messages.body_plain:
I have troubles using irace (version 2.3) in a multi-objective setting. In the first irace-iteration everything works perfect. The target runner puts the obtained solution pool in a file for each candidate configuration and each instance, and the target evaluator then uses this information to determine the hypervolume.

However, in the second iteration something seems to go wrong. The first instance runs smoothly for all candidate configurations. But with the second instance, I can see that the target-runner skips the first two available candidate configurations (the two best/maintained configurations from Iteration 1). However. when calling the target-evaluator, it wants to access the results of these candidate configurations and obviously, irace stops, because target-runner was not run for this instance and candidate configurations.

Could someone help me out with this issue? Am I doing something wrong?
